source_refs.note: Book p. 155-156: 5.6 Angle Between Two Lines, Theorem 7 with proof (Figure 5.8), Corollaries 1 and 2, Examples 12-13 (Figure 5.9)

blocks.text: Let \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) be two intersecting lines \((\ell_1 \nparallel \ell_2)\), which meet at a point \(P\). At the point \(P\) two supplementary angles are formed by the lines \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\).

Unless \(\ell_1 \perp \ell_2\), one of the two angles is acute. The angle from \(\ell_1\) to \(\ell_2\) is the angle \(\theta\) through which \(\ell_1\) is rotated counterclockwise about the point \(P\) so that it coincides with \(\ell_2\).

In the figure below, \(\theta\) is the angle of intersection. It is clear that the inclination of a line is the angle measured in the counterclockwise direction from the positive \(x\)-axis to the line.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two crossing lines make two angles at \(P\), for example \(60^\circ\) and \(120^\circ\); they add up to \(180^\circ\) (supplementary).
To say which one we mean, the book fixes a direction: start on \(\ell_1\) and turn anticlockwise until you lie on \(\ell_2\). That turn is the angle from \(\ell_1\) to \(\ell_2\).
If you start on \(\ell_2\) instead, you get the other angle: the angle from \(\ell_2\) to \(\ell_1\) is \(180^\circ - \theta\). So the order of the two lines matters.
Recall from Unit 5.1: the slope of a line is \(m = \tan\alpha\), where \(\alpha\) is its inclination (\(0^\circ \le \alpha < 180^\circ\)).

Let \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) be two non-vertical lines such that they are not perpendicular to each other. If \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are the slopes of \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) respectively, then the angle \(\theta\) from \(\ell_1\) to \(\ell_2\) is given by

blocks.text_alt: tan theta equals m2 minus m1, over 1 plus m1 m2

blocks.text:
From the figure, we have
\[\alpha_2 = \alpha_1 + \theta\]
or
\[\theta = \alpha_2 - \alpha_1\]
\[\tan\theta = \tan(\alpha_2 - \alpha_1)\]
\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{\tan\alpha_2 - \tan\alpha_1}{1 + \tan\alpha_1\tan\alpha_2}\]
\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{1 + m_1 m_2}\]

blocks.alt: Coordinate axes with origin O. A blue line l1 rises gently to the right and meets the x-axis at angle alpha 1. A green line l2 falls to the right and meets the x-axis at the obtuse angle alpha 2. The lines cross at P, where an arc marks the angle theta turning anticlockwise from l1 to l2.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.8: the angle θ from ℓ₁ to ℓ₂ (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is \(\alpha_2 = \alpha_1 + \theta\)? The two lines and the \(x\)-axis form a triangle. \(\alpha_2\) is an exterior angle of that triangle, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles, here \(\alpha_1\) and \(\theta\).
Then we use the subtraction formula \(\tan(A - B) = \frac{\tan A - \tan B}{1 + \tan A \tan B}\), and replace \(\tan\alpha_1 = m_1\), \(\tan\alpha_2 = m_2\).
Why the conditions? A vertical line has no slope, so \(m\) cannot be used. If the lines are perpendicular, \(1 + m_1 m_2 = 0\) and the fraction has no value (see Corollary 2).

\(\ell_1 \parallel \ell_2\) if and only if \(m_1 = m_2\). Since \(\ell_1 \parallel \ell_2\) so, \(\theta = 0\)
\[\Leftrightarrow \tan\theta = 0 = \dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{1 + m_1 m_2}\]
\[\Leftrightarrow m_2 = m_1\]

\(\ell_1 \perp \ell_2\) iff \(1 + m_1 m_2 = 0\). Since \(\ell_1 \perp \ell_2\) so, \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\)
\[\Leftrightarrow \tan\dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{1 + m_1 m_2} = \infty\]
\[\Leftrightarrow \infty = \dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{1 + m_1 m_2}\]
\(\because \tan\frac{\pi}{2} = \infty\)
\[\Leftrightarrow 1 + m_1 m_2 = 0\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Strictly, \(\tan 90^\circ\) is not a number; it is undefined. The book's \(\infty\) means: as \(\theta\) gets close to \(90^\circ\), \(\tan\theta\) grows without limit. A fraction can only grow without limit when its denominator goes to 0, which is why \(1 + m_1 m_2 = 0\).
A cleaner way: \(\theta = 90^\circ\) exactly when \(\cot\theta = 0\), and \(\cot\theta = \frac{1 + m_1 m_2}{m_2 - m_1}\). This is zero exactly when \(1 + m_1 m_2 = 0\), i.e. \(m_1 m_2 = -1\).
So: parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is \(-1\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
How to use \(\tan\theta = \frac{m_2 - m_1}{1 + m_1 m_2}\):
1. Decide which line you turn from (\(m_1\)) and which you turn to (\(m_2\)). The 'to' slope comes first in the numerator.
2. If \(\tan\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is acute: \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(\tan\theta)\).
3. If \(\tan\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) is obtuse: \(\theta = 180^\circ - \tan^{-1}|\tan\theta|\).
4. The acute angle between the lines is always \(\tan^{-1}\left|\frac{m_2 - m_1}{1 + m_1 m_2}\right|\).

blocks.title: Example 12
blocks.problem: Find the angle from the line with slope \(-\frac{7}{3}\) to the line with slope \(\frac{5}{2}\).
steps:
Given: slope of the first line \(m_1 = -\frac{7}{3}\), slope of the second line \(m_2 = \frac{5}{2}\).
To find: the angle \(\theta\) from the first line to the second line.
Method: Theorem 7, \(\tan\theta = \frac{m_2 - m_1}{1 + m_1 m_2}\). The line we turn from gives \(m_1\); the line we turn to gives \(m_2\).

Step 1: the numerator
\[m_2 - m_1 = \dfrac{5}{2} - \left(-\dfrac{7}{3}\right)\]
\[= \dfrac{15 + 14}{6} = \dfrac{29}{6}\]
Why: subtracting a negative number adds it; the common denominator of 2 and 3 is 6.

Step 2: the denominator
\[1 + m_1 m_2 = 1 + \left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)\left(-\dfrac{7}{3}\right)\]
\[= 1 - \dfrac{35}{6} = -\dfrac{29}{6}\]
Why: the product of a positive and a negative slope is negative, and \(1 = \frac{6}{6}\).

Step 3: divide
\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{29/6}{-29/6} = \dfrac{29}{-29} = -1\]
\[\Rightarrow \tan\theta = -1\]
Why: the two 6s cancel, as in the book's working.

Step 4: read off the angle
\[\theta = 180^\circ - 45^\circ\]
\[\theta = 135^\circ\]
Why: \(\tan 45^\circ = 1\). A negative tangent means the angle is obtuse (between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\)), so \(\theta = 180^\circ - 45^\circ\).

Check:
\[\tan 135^\circ = -\tan 45^\circ = -1 \;\checkmark\]
The acute angle between the two lines is \(45^\circ\), and \(45^\circ + 135^\circ = 180^\circ\), as two supplementary angles should.

blocks.title: Example 13
blocks.problem: Find the angles of the triangle whose vertices are \(A(1, 2)\), \(B(7, 3)\) and \(C(4, 9)\).
steps:
Given: \(A(1, 2)\), \(B(7, 3)\), \(C(4, 9)\).
To find: the angles \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) of the triangle.
Method: find the slopes of the three sides, then use Theorem 7 at each vertex. The vertices \(A \to B \to C\) go round anticlockwise (Figure 5.9), so each interior angle is measured anticlockwise: \(A\) from \(AB\) to \(AC\), \(B\) from \(BC\) to \(BA\), \(C\) from \(CA\) to \(CB\).

Step 1: slopes of the sides
Let the slopes of \(AB\), \(BC\) and \(CA\) be \(m_c\), \(m_a\) and \(m_b\) (each named after the side opposite a vertex: \(a = BC\), \(b = CA\), \(c = AB\)).
\[m_a = \dfrac{9 - 3}{4 - 7} = \dfrac{6}{-3} = -2\]
\[m_b = \dfrac{2 - 9}{1 - 4} = \dfrac{-7}{-3} = \dfrac{7}{3}\]
\[m_c = \dfrac{3 - 2}{7 - 1} = \dfrac{1}{6}\]
Why: slope \(= \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}\) for each pair of end points.

Step 2: angle \(A\), measured from \(\overline{AB}\) to \(\overline{AC}\)
The book prints: \(\tan A = \frac{m_c - m_b}{1 + m_c m_b} = -\frac{39}{25}\), then \(A = 57.35^\circ\).
Working it out (turning from \(AB\), slope \(m_c\), to \(AC\), slope \(m_b\)):
\[\tan A = \dfrac{m_b - m_c}{1 + m_b m_c}\]
\[= \dfrac{\frac{7}{3} - \frac{1}{6}}{1 + \left(\frac{7}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)}\]
\[= \dfrac{13/6}{25/18} = \dfrac{39}{25}\]
\[\Rightarrow A = 57.34^\circ\]
Why: in Theorem 7 the slope of the line we turn to comes first. The book's order gives \(-\frac{39}{25}\), which is the angle from \(AC\) to \(AB\) (\(122.66^\circ\)), not \(A\). Its value \(A \approx 57.3^\circ\) is right because it took the positive value.

Step 3: angle \(B\), measured from \(\overline{BC}\) to \(\overline{AB}\)
\[\tan B = \dfrac{m_c - m_a}{1 + m_c m_a}\]
\[= \dfrac{\frac{1}{6} - (-2)}{1 + \left(\frac{1}{6}\right)(-2)}\]
\[= \dfrac{13/6}{4/6} = \dfrac{13}{4}\]
The book prints: \(B = 72.87^\circ\); \(\tan^{-1}\frac{13}{4} = 72.90^\circ\) to two decimal places.
Why: here we turn from \(BC\) (slope \(m_a\)) to \(BA\) (slope \(m_c\)), so \(m_c\) comes first, exactly as the book writes.

Step 4: angle \(C\), measured from \(\overline{AC}\) to \(\overline{BC}\)
\[\tan C = \dfrac{m_a - m_b}{1 + m_a m_b}\]
\[= \dfrac{-2 - \frac{7}{3}}{1 + (-2)\left(\frac{7}{3}\right)}\]
\[= \dfrac{-13/3}{-11/3} = \dfrac{13}{11}\]
The book prints: \(C = 49.78^\circ\); \(\tan^{-1}\frac{13}{11} = 49.76^\circ\) to two decimal places.
Why: we turn from \(CA\) (slope \(m_b\)) to \(CB\) (slope \(m_a\)), so \(m_a\) comes first.

Check:
\[57.34^\circ + 72.90^\circ + 49.76^\circ = 180^\circ \;\checkmark\]
All three tangents are positive, so all three angles are acute, which matches Figure 5.9.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
In Example 13 the book says angle \(A\) is measured from \(AB\) to \(AC\) but writes \(\tan A = \frac{m_c - m_b}{1 + m_c m_b} = -\frac{39}{25}\). That order gives the angle from \(AC\) to \(AB\). The correct line is \(\tan A = \frac{m_b - m_c}{1 + m_b m_c} = \frac{39}{25}\), so \(A = 57.34^\circ\).
The printed decimals are slightly off: \(\tan^{-1}\frac{39}{25} = 57.34^\circ\) (printed \(57.35^\circ\)), \(\tan^{-1}\frac{13}{4} = 72.90^\circ\) (printed \(72.87^\circ\)), \(\tan^{-1}\frac{13}{11} = 49.76^\circ\) (printed \(49.78^\circ\)). Both sets add up to \(180^\circ\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. The angle from \(\ell_1\) to \(\ell_2\) is the anticlockwise turn that takes \(\ell_1\) onto \(\ell_2\).
2. Theorem 7: \(\tan\theta = \frac{m_2 - m_1}{1 + m_1 m_2}\), with \(m_2\) the slope of the line you turn to.
3. Parallel: \(m_1 = m_2\). Perpendicular: \(m_1 m_2 = -1\).
4. \(\tan\theta < 0\) means \(\theta\) is obtuse: \(\theta = 180^\circ - \tan^{-1}|\tan\theta|\).
5. For a triangle, go round the vertices anticlockwise and measure each angle from the side to the next vertex to the side to the previous vertex.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Swapping \(m_1\) and \(m_2\): this gives \(180^\circ - \theta\) instead of \(\theta\) (the slip in the book's Example 13).
2. Taking \(\tan^{-1}\) of a negative value on the calculator and writing a negative angle; add \(180^\circ\) to get the angle between \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\).
3. Using Theorem 7 when \(1 + m_1 m_2 = 0\); then the lines are simply perpendicular and \(\theta = 90^\circ\).
4. Using it for a vertical line: a vertical line has no slope, its inclination is \(90^\circ\), so work with inclinations instead.
